Description: Beats per minute at rest, in activity or overnight. The most commonly synced measure and the one most apps lead with.
Coding note: Also the FHIR vital-signs code. | Resting heart rate: same metric, different code. Keep as a variant, not a separate data point.

Description: Variation between consecutive beats, used as a general recovery and autonomic stress indicator.
Coding note: Wearables report SDNN or RMSSD and the two are not interchangeable: record which one in the metric definition.

Description: Systolic and diastolic from a cuff, usually logged together with the pulse. Orthostatic pairs matter for some conditions.
Code display: Blood pressure panel with all children optional
Other codings: LOINC 8480-6 Systolic blood pressure [mm[Hg]] (component); LOINC 8462-4 Diastolic blood pressure [mm[Hg]] (component)

Description: A recorded waveform plus the rhythm classification derived from it. Stored as a file, not a number.
Percentage saturation, spot-checked or sampled through the night.
Code display: Oxygen saturation in Arterial blood by Pulse oximetry
Other codings: LOINC 2708-6 Oxygen saturation in Arterial blood [%] (variant)
Coding note: Pulse oximetry is the right method for a wearable or finger clip. | Generic form; use only if the source gives no method.

Description: Breaths per minute, generally derived overnight by a wearable rather than measured directly.
Lung function measures from a meter: peak expiratory flow, FEV1.
Coding note: This row covers two measures. Split into peak flow and FEV1 (candidate 20150-9, L) when coding for real.

Description: Fingerstick readings or a continuous sensor stream. One metric, two very different data shapes.
Coding note: Code depends on specimen, method and unit. Candidates: 15074-8 blood mmol/L, 41653-7 capillary by glucometer mg/dL. Pick by what the source device reports.

Description: Blood or urine strip result.
Code display: Ketones in Urine by Test strip (to confirm)
Coding note: Urine strip only. Blood ketone (beta-hydroxybutyrate) needs its own code, found at verification.

Description: Scale reading. The trend carries the information; any single value is noise.
Fat, muscle, water and bone mass, usually from a bioimpedance scale.
Coding note: Only body fat has a clean code. Muscle, water and bone mass should become their own metrics before they are coded.

Description: An absolute reading, or a deviation from your own established baseline.
Coding note: Skin-temperature deviation from baseline is a different metric and needs its own entry.

Description: Changes almost never, but needed for BMI and for dosing.
Any analyte from a blood or urine panel, with its unit and reference range. Same shape as a home reading; only the source differs.
Millilitres over a period. Sits in Vitals rather than Lifestyle because sustained high output is a clinical dehydration risk.
What you have been diagnosed with, its onset date, and whether it is active or resolved. One of the two things a clinician asks for first.
Start, end and outcome. An interval, like any other condition.
Hereditary risk: the relative, the condition, and their age at onset.
Substance, the reaction it causes and how severe. Must be reachable instantly, including from the emergency view.
Non-immune reactions to food or medication. Clinically distinct from allergy, even if the words get used loosely.
Date, facility, surgeon, and anything implanted or created - including the stoma formation itself.
Admission and discharge dates with the reason. Rarely read, must never be lost.
Vaccine, date, product and lot, plus when the next dose is due.
A scheduled visit with prep instructions and the questions you want to ask. The one item here that points forward rather than back.
What happened at a past appointment, what was said and what changed as a result.
A clinician or clinic: specialty, contact details, and your own notes on them.
Lab reports, letters, discharge summaries. Attaches to the record it belongs to rather than floating free.
The radiologist's report plus the image files themselves, which are large and rarely opened.
A permanent attribute whose only real use is the emergency view.
Coding note: Two metrics: ABO group and Rh (candidate 10331-7).

Description: Policy, claims, what is reimbursable and what you have already paid.
Hours slept and the schedule you kept. Behaviour you control, judged against your own target rather than a clinical band.
Deep, light, REM and awake time as estimated by a wearable.
Your own verdict on the night, which frequently explains what the numbers cannot.
Daily count. The default ambient activity measure that every device supplies.
Code display: Number of steps in unspecified time Pedometer

Description: Type, duration, intensity and route. Sets, reps and load where it is strength work.
Calories burned beyond resting metabolism. Computed from movement and heart rate rather than measured.
What you ate and when. The highest-friction entry in any health app, which is why photo and barcode entry exist.
Fluid volume and type. Carries more weight than usual with an ostomy, where intake and output have to balance.
Amount and timing. Both correlate strongly enough with sleep and HRV to be worth separating from general intake.
A daily self-rating as part of a check-in rather than a clinical assessment. A clinical mood problem is recorded as a Symptom instead.
Self-rated, or inferred by a wearable from heart rate variability.
Duration and type, sometimes with the physiological response alongside.
Phase and flow. Not behaviour, but a daily log without a clinical band, so the axis places it here.
When the pouch was changed, which product was used, and whether it was scheduled or forced by a leak.
How long an appliance stayed on. Computed from consecutive change events, and the headline outcome for comparing products.
Frequency and timing across the day.
Barrier ring, paste, powder, adhesive remover - what went on alongside the appliance.
When and where a seal failed. The event you most want to drive toward zero, and the clearest signal a product is wrong.
A Bristol-style ordinal scale for stoma or bowel output, logged alongside volume.
Explains sudden shifts in sleep, activity and almost every other metric.
Temperature, humidity, pollen, air quality. Correlation context rather than a destination of its own.
What you felt and how severe, with a timestamp. The generic record the whole category is built on.
A period rather than a moment, with a start, an end and a severity curve. A different record shape from a point log.
What you believe set a symptom off. The input side of every correlation the app will run.
A picture of the same site over time, which communicates change better than any written score.
Often the most actionable subjective measure in chronic illness, and the hardest to capture consistently.
Self-reported feeling, distinct from the thermometer reading that belongs in Vitals.
Awareness of the heartbeat - racing, skipping or pounding. Worth logging separately from any ECG it prompts.
At rest or on exertion, which are clinically quite different things.
An episode with onset, duration and intensity, frequently worth its own focused view.
Self-rated clarity and concentration.
Lightheadedness or vertigo, often tied to hydration or blood pressure.
Severity and its relation to meals or medication timing.
Location, intensity and quality, usually entered on a body map rather than typed.
Code display: Pain severity - 0-10 verbal numeric rating [Score] - Reported
Coding note: Severity only. Location is a SNOMED body-structure concept, handled when symptoms are coded.

Description: Rash, irritation or healing, tracked more reliably with serial photos than with words.
Irritation, burning or soreness around the stoma, as you experience it rather than as it is scored.
The drug itself: name, strength, form, route and the reason you take it. A catalogue entry, not an event.
A planned dose at a time of day, which is what the reminder and the daily plan are built from.
What actually happened. The skipped case carries as much information as the taken one and is missed by most apps.
PRN medication. How often you reach for it is clinically meaningful in its own right.
Vitamins and non-prescription products, modelled the same way as medication.
An unwanted effect linked back to a specific drug and dose rather than floating loose as a symptom.
A defined period on a therapy, with a start and an end.
Physio, psychology, dental or any recurring non-drug care appointment that is treatment rather than consultation.
The appliance as a catalogue entry: brand, reference code, convexity, flange size, barrier type. The single most important thing not to model as free text.
Rings, pastes and sprays, each with their own reference and attributes.
CPAP, pump, CGM and similar, with their settings and their own consumables.
How many you have left and the reorder threshold. A running quantity rather than a fixed property.
Where supplies come from: contact, lead time, and what they are allowed to bill.
A dated order with quantities, cost and coverage.
A labelled interval on one configuration, so outcomes compare period against period instead of being averaged across every change you have ever made.
